setupLevel: LAB-1 Basic - ticker, date, time, and timeframe

chapterTitle: Day Trading, Swing Trading, Scalping, Momentum, and More
concept: Holding Horizon: Day Trade vs. Scalp vs. Swing
setupLevel: LAB-1 Classification — ticker, date, time, and timeframe; no studies
studies: None added. Keep your attention on the style-classification task.
goal: Classify hypothetical plans by intended holding period without using the chart as an entry signal.
beforeAdvance: Pause at 9:30 a.m. ET. Confirm AMZN, May 6, 2024, ET, and the 5-minute chart. Read the decision descriptions before advancing. The chart is context only; this chapter is not teaching candle interpretation or an entry setup.
practiceSteps: Advance only through 10:00 a.m. ET. Use the chart only to support the style-classification exercise, not to grade AMZN as a trade.
Plan A says: open after 9:30 a.m. and close before the same trading day ends. Classify the holding-period style as day trading.
Plan B says: open and attempt to close within only a few minutes. Classify the holding-period style as scalping, which is also intraday.
Plan C says: open today with an explicit plan to hold across several sessions if its later-defined thesis remains valid. Classify the holding-period style as swing trading.
Notice that the same security can support different style labels because the label describes the plan—not an identity permanently attached to AMZN.

chapterTitle: Day Trading, Swing Trading, Scalping, Momentum, and More
concept: Style vs. Approach vs. Setup vs. Context
setupLevel: LAB-1 Classification — ticker, date, time, and timeframe; no studies
studies: None added. Keep your attention on the style-classification task.
goal: Practice attaching the correct kind of label to a hypothetical trading plan without turning the historical chart into a setup lesson.
beforeAdvance: Pause at 9:30 a.m. ET. Confirm AMD, May 6, 2024, ET, and the 5-minute chart. Read the decision descriptions before advancing. The chart is context only; this chapter is not teaching candle interpretation or an entry setup.
practiceSteps: Advance only through 10:00 a.m. ET. Observe that price changes over the interval, but keep the exercise focused on style classification rather than candle or volume interpretation.
Hypothetical Plan A says only: “Any position must be closed today.” That statement defines holding horizon—day trading—but says nothing about setup.
Hypothetical Plan B adds: “I am interested only if directional movement is already strong.” That adds a momentum approach, but it still does not define an executable entry.

Hypothetical Plan C adds: “I will later require a defined breakout condition.” Breakout is now a setup-family label, but your job here is only to classify the plan—not to decide whether a breakout actually exists on the chart.
Write the four questions beside the chart: How long? What behavior? What setup family? What context? If a label does not answer the same question, do not treat it as a competing style.

concept: Identify premarket, the regular-market open, the regular-market close, and after-hours on one historical trading day
setupLevel: LAB-1 Session Map — ticker, date, ET clock, timeframe, and extended-session display; no studies
goal: Learn where the sessions begin and end on the clock without interpreting price behavior.
beforeAdvance: Confirm NVDA, May 6, 2024, ET, the 5-minute chart, and the extended-hours display. This is a clock-and-session exercise only.
practiceSteps: Start at 8:00 a.m. ET and advance only through 8:10 a.m. ET. Label that window premarket. Stop there.
Use Reset Time or controlled navigation to move to 9:25 a.m. ET. Advance through 9:35 a.m. ET and identify the 9:30 a.m. boundary between premarket and regular market hours.
Move to 3:55 p.m. ET. Advance through 4:10 p.m. ET and identify the 4:00 p.m. boundary between regular market hours and the post-market/after-hours period.
Write the three boundaries in your notes: premarket is before 9:30 a.m.; regular market hours are 9:30 a.m.–4:00 p.m.; post-market activity follows 4:00 p.m. on venues that support it.
At this stage, compare only the session windows and their clock boundaries. We will add time-of-day behavior and extended-hours risk next.
Remember that this is a May 2024 historical session. It cannot display Nasdaq’s December 2026 Night Session because that exchange session did not exist on the historical date.
additionalNotes: Chart Setting: Use the cog icon → Chart Settings → Equities → Show Extended-Hours Trading session. Highlighting the extended session is optional.
Window A — Premarket: Start 8:00 a.m. ET → End 8:10 a.m. ET
Window B — Open Transition: Start 9:25 a.m. ET → End 9:35 a.m. ET
Window C — Close Transition: Start 3:55 p.m. ET → End 4:10 p.m. ET

Reset to noon and watch 12:00 to 12:30 p.m. ET. Use the same plain-language description.
Compare the two observations. If they differ, write “time of day changed the environment on this session.” If they do not, write “this session did not follow the broad tendency strongly.”
Do not conclude that NFLX always behaves this way at the open or at midday. One day is an example, not a statistical rule.
additionalNotes: Window A — Opening Minutes: Start 9:30 a.m. ET → End 10:00 a.m. ET
Window B — Midday Comparison: Start 12:00 p.m. ET → End 12:30 p.m. ET

concept: Bid, Ask, Last, Spread, and Midpoint in a Frequently Updating Quote
setupLevel: LAB-1 Quote Mechanics — ticker, date, ET clock, 5-minute chart, Level 1 quote fields; no studies
goal: Identify the quote fields and calculate spread/midpoint without turning the quote into an entry signal.
beforeAdvance: Confirm ticker, date, ET, 5-minute chart, and a Level 1 quote display that shows Bid, Ask, Last, and Size. Stop at the listed starting boundary.
practiceSteps: Pause at 9:45 a.m. ET. In a Level 1 quote display, record Bid, Ask, Last, Bid Size, Ask Size, and Last Size exactly as your platform displays them.
Calculate Ask − Bid. That is the spread for that snapshot.
Calculate (Bid + Ask) ÷ 2. That is the midpoint for that snapshot.
Compare Last with Bid, Ask, and Midpoint. State where Last sits without predicting the next trade.
Advance toward 9:50 a.m. ET and repeat the observation once. Notice that quote prices and sizes can update even when you have not changed anything.
Describe the quote itself without assigning a bullish or bearish prediction.

Foundation Deep-Dive: Moving Averages Smooth Price at the Cost of Lag The basic question: What does average price over a defined number of periods look like as new data arrives? A moving average recalculates as new bars are added and old bars leave the lookback. A simple moving average weights observations equally. An exponential moving average gives more weight to recent data and responds more quickly. Length creates a trade-off. Shorter averages respond faster but can change direction frequently. Longer averages are smoother but react more slowly. Price crossovers and moving-average crossovers can be described objectively but can whipsaw in sideways markets. Combine the average with structure, location, and market condition rather than using it as a command. How This Shows Up in Real Trading Buying every cross above an average can create repeated whipsaw losses. Treating a moving average as guaranteed support can encourage holding after structure fails. Before You Move On Explain an SMA and the basic difference from an EMA. Explain responsiveness versus smoothness. Use slope and price relationship as context rather than entries by themselves.

Foundation Deep-Dive: VWAP Is a Session Benchmark, Not a Prediction Line The basic question: What is the volume-weighted average price of the session up to this point? VWAP combines price and volume so prices associated with more traded volume have more influence on the cumulative average. Standard session VWAP typically resets according to its defined anchor rather than using a fixed rolling number of bars. Price above VWAP means current price is above that cumulative benchmark; below means it is below. Reclaim, rejection, failure, and chop labels organize observed interactions but require explicit rules. VWAP can help with continuation context when price, structure, volume, and the VWAP relationship support the same direction. The line itself does not create guaranteed support, resistance, fair value, or a magnet. How This Shows Up in Real Trading Buying every VWAP cross can create repeated losses during chop. Calling VWAP support merely because price touched it exaggerates what the calculation proves. Before You Move On Explain what volume-weighted means. Distinguish cumulative VWAP from a fixed-length moving average. Classify price/VWAP relationships without turning the line into a command.
